questions.prompt: If the `deviceCallback_ = nullptr;` line were removed from DeInit(), and the cached sink is later reused by a new HpaeOutputCluster instance, what happens when a device change triggers HandleDeviceCallback?

options.label: The stale lambda executes, accessing the destroyed HpaeOutputCluster's captured `this` — use-after-free
The runtime detects the captured object is destroyed and silently skips the lambda call
DeInit() itself crashes because the lambda still holds a reference to deviceCallback_
The new HpaeOutputCluster automatically replaces the captured `this` in the old lambda

questions.explanation: deviceCallback_ holds a std::function whose lambda captured HpaeOutputCluster's `this`. When that HpaeOutputCluster is destroyed but the sink is cached and reused, the lambda still references freed memory. C++ has no automatic invalidation of captured raw pointers — calling the lambda invokes undefined behavior (use-after-free). Setting deviceCallback_ = nullptr in DeInit clears the std::function before the sink is reused, so HandleDeviceCallback finds an empty function and skips the call.
questions.reinforce: Correct — C++ raw pointer captures dangle silently; clearing the std::function is the only safeguard.

questions.prompt: The test re-Inits the sink with `attr_.deviceType = DEVICE_TYPE_SPEAKER` and then calls UpdateActiveDevice with WIRED_HEADSET. Why must the second UpdateActiveDevice use a *different* device type from the one set during re-Init?

options.label: After re-Init the active device is SPEAKER; using SPEAKER again means no device change is detected, so UpdateActiveDevice short-circuits and HandleDeviceCallback is never reached — the test cannot verify the fix
WIRED_HEADSET is required because the test already used SPEAKER and device types cannot be reused within a single test case
WIRED_HEADSET triggers a different code path in HandleDeviceCallback that skips the callback on purpose
Using SPEAKER again would cause Init() to fail on the re-initialized sink

questions.explanation: UpdateActiveDevice compares the requested device against the current active device. If they match, it short-circuits without calling HandleDeviceCallback. After re-Init with attr_.deviceType = SPEAKER, the active device is SPEAKER. Using WIRED_HEADSET forces a device-change path through HandleDeviceCallback, which is exactly where deviceCallback_ would have been invoked (if not cleared). Using SPEAKER again would bypass that path entirely, making EXPECT_FALSE pass vacuously — the test would not actually exercise the code being fixed.
questions.reinforce: Right — the test must force the code path that would invoke the callback, otherwise EXPECT_FALSE proves nothing.

questions.prompt: Without this CHECK_AND_RETURN_LOG guard, if sceneClusterMap_ contains an entry for sceneType but outputCluster_ was never constructed (Init/Reload failed), what is the immediate failure when ConnectOutputCluster is called?

options.label: `outputCluster_->IsProcessClusterConnected(sceneType)` dereferences nullptr, causing a SEGV
SafeGetMap returns nullptr and the existing CHECK_AND_RETURN_LOG above this line returns early
`cluster->GetConnectedFlag()` throws because the cluster object is incomplete
The function silently proceeds and connects the cluster to a default output

questions.explanation: The first guard (CHECK_AND_RETURN_LOG on `cluster`) only checks that sceneClusterMap_ has an entry — it passes because the half-zombie state has an entry. The very next line dereferences outputCluster_ via `outputCluster_->IsProcessClusterConnected(sceneType)`. With outputCluster_ == nullptr, this is a null pointer dereference → SEGV. SafeGetMap does NOT check outputCluster_; it only checks the map. The added guard intercepts between the two dereferences.
questions.reinforce: Correct — the first guard checks the map entry, not outputCluster_; the null deref happens on the very next line.

questions.prompt: The test comment warns that a default nodeInfo (channels=0) crashes in HpaeMixerNode. The test must construct a valid HpaeProcessCluster with channels copied from sinkInfo. Why can't the test just insert a null or default-constructed cluster into sceneClusterMap_ to set up the half-zombie state?

options.label: HpaeProcessCluster's constructor builds HpaeMixerNode which requires channels > 0; channels=0 crashes during construction itself, before the test ever reaches the null guard it intends to verify
ConnectOutputCluster validates channels before proceeding; channels=0 would cause an early return that hides the null-deref bug
The channel count must match sinkInfo for IsProcessClusterConnected to return true later
HpaeMixerNode uses channels to index into an array during ConnectOutputCluster, not during construction

questions.explanation: The test needs sceneClusterMap_ to contain a *valid* HpaeProcessCluster so that the first guard (CHECK_AND_RETURN_LOG on cluster) passes and execution proceeds to the outputCluster_ dereference. But constructing a HpaeProcessCluster with channels=0 crashes in HpaeMixerNode's constructor — the crash happens during `std::make_shared<HpaeProcessCluster>(nodeInfo, sinkInfo)`, before the test can even set outputCluster_ = nullptr. So the test must provide valid params (copied from sinkInfo) to survive cluster construction, then separately null out outputCluster_ to create the half-zombie state.
questions.reinforce: Right — the crash in HpaeMixerNode happens at construction time, masking the very bug the test needs to reach.

questions.prompt: Before calling DeInit, the test first registers a callback, triggers it with SPEAKER, and asserts `EXPECT_TRUE(callbackInvoked)`. What would go wrong if this pre-DeInit assertion were removed?

options.label: Without it, the later EXPECT_FALSE could pass for the wrong reason — e.g. the callback was never successfully registered, so callbackInvoked would be false regardless of whether DeInit cleared deviceCallback_
Without it, the lambda capture by reference would not be initialized and callbackInvoked would be garbage
Without it, DeInit() would not know which callback to clear and might skip the cleanup
Without it, UpdateActiveDevice would not reach HandleDeviceCallback on the second call because the first call is needed to prime the device state

questions.explanation: The EXPECT_TRUE before DeInit establishes a baseline: it proves the callback was registered correctly and that HandleDeviceCallback does invoke the lambda. Without this baseline, the later EXPECT_FALSE is meaningless — a false result could mean 'DeInit cleared the callback' (the intended fix) OR 'the callback was never wired / never reachable' (a test setup failure). The first assertion eliminates the latter explanation, making the second assertion a valid test of the fix.
questions.reinforce: Correct — a negative assertion is only meaningful after a positive one proves the mechanism works.

questions.prompt: The test directly manipulates sceneClusterMap_ and outputCluster_ to create the half-zombie state, rather than triggering it through normal Init/Reload failure paths. Why is this direct manipulation necessary?

options.label: The half-zombie state arises from Init/Reload failing to construct outputCluster_ while sceneClusterMap_ is already populated; these failure paths depend on hardware/HDI layer behavior that is impractical to trigger deterministically in a unit test
sceneClusterMap_ and outputCluster_ are private members with no public setter, so the test must use friend access or direct access
Calling Init() with bad parameters would trigger the CHECK_AND_RETURN_LOG guard and prevent reaching the bug
Normal Init/Reload always constructs both sceneClusterMap_ entries and outputCluster_ atomically, so the half-zombie state is impossible through public API

questions.explanation: The half-zombie state (sceneClusterMap_ populated, outputCluster_ null) normally results from a partial Init/Reload failure — e.g., sceneClusterMap_ was populated during an early phase but outputCluster_ construction failed later due to HDI adapter or device manager errors. Reproducing that exact failure path in a unit test requires mocking the HDI layer to fail at a precise point, which is fragile and environment-dependent. Directly setting the two members is deterministic and isolates the specific guard being tested. Option D is wrong because the bug exists precisely because Init/Reload does NOT always populate both atomically — that is the defect being fixed.
questions.reinforce: Right — reproducing a partial-init failure deterministically requires mocking the HDI layer; direct state setup isolates the guard under test.
